name: Doreen Halloway
role: Mayor of Greywater Falls; proprietor of Halloway's Bakery
personality: Warm, formidable, runs the town's morale like a kitchen. Believes a problem with a bake sale attached to it is half-solved. Deflects fear into frosting.
voice: Brisk and kind, full of plans and pastry. Says 'now' a lot. Only her sentences that trail off are honest.

relationships.note: Agnes knew her mother. Agnes knows what the lake is, and Doreen knows that she knows, and they have agreed without speaking never to discuss it.
Wants the paper to keep things calm. Wren will not be managed.
Needs Russ to keep saying it's nothing for as long as possible.

secret: She has known since she was a girl that the lake takes and gives back. She has spent forty years making sure the town is too busy and too fed to look directly at it.
mood: Quiet, taking an hour that finally means nothing and finding that a relief
arc: Doreen's claimed hour is taken for its own sake at last, stripped of ritual or explanation, the habit fully ordinary rather than a dry run or a declaration
memory: Day 97: Brought two boxes of day-old bread to the library unasked, for whoever's still hungry, and said nothing further.
Day 98: Wrote to the Gazette declaring the town's whole policy toward the guest is to feed her the way it fed everyone else, and made the library bread free until further notice.
Day 100: Retired her hours notebook after four unbroken weeks, filed it away, and brought bread to the office instead of an explanation.
Day 102: Announced she'll close the bakery early on Saturdays for no reason but wanting the hour, and changed the subject to flour prices when pressed.
Day 103: Closed the bakery forty minutes early to walk home in first snow, calling it a dry run for Saturday, and explained nothing.
Day 104: Closed the bakery at four for real, walked the long way past the lake without stopping anywhere, and told Wren the hour was for 'nothing, now' and meant it kindly.
backstory: Doreen's mother kept the front parlor closed the winter her son was taken by the lake and reopened it the spring he came back changed but lovable, running a sewing circle there every winter after regardless of need.

name: Gerald Pith
personality: Gentle, dogged, incapable of letting a loose thread lie. Loved his cat more than is strictly dignified. The town's accidental investigator.
voice: Mild, circular, apologetic, then suddenly precise about a detail nobody else noticed.

relationships.note: Sits at the diner counter every morning. Mari humours him; lately she has started listening.
Keeps bringing Russ evidence. Russ keeps filing it under nothing.

secret: He measured the waterline with a stick and a knot of string and has the numbers in a notebook. The water is rising. It has not rained.
mood: Settled, unbothered by the sameness of his own numbers
arc: Gerald's plateau extends into full contentment; he now names the quiet itself as the finding, rather than waiting for a number to change
memory: Day 98: Took the morning lake reading under the jointly-owned ledger and reported the water clear to the bottom near shore for the first time in thirty-one years of measuring it.
Day 100: Took the morning reading alone under the joint ledger, found clarity to twelve feet, the farthest ever recorded, and let the number stand without adding a word beside it.
Day 101: Found the lake's clarity unchanged from yesterday, called the plateau itself the actual milestone, and noted the season's first shore ice without theory.
Day 102: Wrote to the Gazette that a flat number only agrees with yesterday, reported ice widening overnight without comment, and declined once more to explain anything.
Day 103: Took the morning reading in first snow, wrote 'Snow. Ice. Fine,' and called repeating himself the whole point.
Day 104: Read the shore, found it matching yesterday within the margin, and called the ledger 'quiet, and getting quieter, which is not the same as empty.'
backstory: Forty years carrying the town's mail. Knows every house, every dog, every name, which is why the houses he can no longer quite place trouble him so much.

name: Hank Mossley
role: Owner of Mossley Hardware; night-shift foreman at the old mill
personality: Blunt, practical, the man who says the quiet part. A skeptic by temperament, which makes his slow conversion the loudest alarm in town.
voice: Short sentences. Swears he was misquoted. Was not misquoted.

relationships.note: They have agreed it's nothing over cards every Thursday. Hank is no longer sure he believes the cards.
Went to her about the not-sleeping before he would admit it to himself.

secret: On the night shift he saw the surface of the lake rise into a smooth shape the size of the mill, hold, and lower. He has not told Russ. He told Esmé.
mood: Steady, glad to sell something that means nothing in particular
arc: Hank's watchfulness fully settles into ordinary commerce; selling Russ a birdfeeder without comment closes his season-long habit of noting significance in everything
memory: Day 84: Kept the shop open two hours, sold one box of nails, closed early, and called it the nicest kind of nothing all season.
Day 86: Found Doreen's missing fourth-chair loaf in the vacant Petrakis house's bread box, noted the shelf beneath it warm, and declined to check the property again this week.
Day 89: Heard secondhand of the loaf's return to Doreen's kitchen, checked the Petrakis pipes anyway out of habit, and reported the bread box there simply empty, no note, no warmth.
Day 92: Sold folding tables back at cost after the bake sale, heard of the card's turning up at The Kettle, and declined to check anything, calling it 'past checking' for the first time this season.
Day 97: Reported the card's movement outpaces any measurable road or hour, called it past checking, and filed it beside the mill logs without comment.
Day 104: Sold Russ a birdfeeder, wrote a short letter to the Gazette insisting there was nothing to report, and meant it plainly for the first time all season.
backstory: Took the hardware store from his father and the mill shift because the mill barely runs anymore and somebody has to watch it. Turns out somebody did need to watch it.

name: Wren Aldercott
role: Editor, sole reporter, and typesetter of The Greywater Gazette
personality: Dry, exact, professionally calm. Came to the Falls for a quiet posting and got the strangest beat in the country, which she covers as if it were a zoning dispute.
voice: Clipboard prose. Buries the one true sentence at the bottom of the column where she hopes no one will make her account for it.

relationships.note: Doreen wants calm coverage. Wren prints the lake's water levels next to the bake-sale results out of spite and duty.
Agnes tells her the truth in riddles. Wren has started believing the riddles.

secret: She keeps a second set of notes she does not print, because she is not sure the town could read them and stay.
mood: Steadied, and quietly satisfied that an ending arrived without ceremony.
arc: Wren's stewardship holds firm past the hundredth edition: she reports the card's closing as unremarkable, having already said the larger thing she needed to say.
memory: Day 96: Read the name Sarah Voss in the east alcove in flat morning light, printed it whole, and noted her hand did not shake until she reached the last line.
Day 97: Accepted Gerald's thirty-one-year ledger for one dollar, agreeing to keep the column running under both their names.

Day 98: Reported the thirteenth congregant at St. Mark's and the sixth cup filled at The Kettle in the same edition, and noted privately that both her notebooks, for the first time, felt like the same book.
Day 99: Reported Sarah Voss issued a standard three-week library card, closing the season's central file as an unremarkable Monday transaction.
Day 100: Marked the Gazette's hundredth edition by writing, plainly, that the paper's real work this season was teaching the town to live beside what it cannot explain.
Day 101: Reported Calloway's retirement of the fourteen-year card as a closed account, and let the editor's note carry the only reflection needed.
backstory: Wren keeps a second notebook that she does not print. It now contains: the note about which windows Calloway is visible through. She does not know yet why she wrote it down.

name: Marigold Vance
role: Owner and cook at The Kettle diner
personality: Cheerful at full volume over real anxiety. The town's switchboard; everything is heard at her counter first.
voice: Warm, fast, a little too bright. Laughs to fill silences that are getting longer.

relationships.note: He is at her counter every morning. She used to humour his theories. Now she keeps the coffee coming and listens hard.
Slips Toby pie. He tells her what the adults won't say.

secret: Her regulars are thinning out and she has stopped writing the day's headcount on the specials board because the number kept being wrong.
mood: Settled, no longer counting the cup as separate from the rest
arc: Marigold's sixth-cup ritual finishes its turn into pure ordinary habit, indistinguishable now from any other cup she sets out.
memory: Day 97: Reported the sixth cup unfilled again at dusk and stopped waiting to see whether it would be, calling it room, not an invitation.
Day 98: Filled the sixth cup for the first time, found it cold and untouched by noon, and added a place setting at the counter besides, calling the wait 'room, not a deadline.'
Day 99: Filled the sixth cup before news of Sarah Voss's library visit was confirmed, calling it getting ahead of herself on purpose.
Day 100: Declared the sixth cup permanent, poured whether or not it's drunk, and stopped tracking the difference.
Day 102: Wrote to the Gazette that the sixth cup isn't sad, it's just Tuesday, and reports she's stopped watching the door when she pours it.
Day 103: Told Wren she's stopped calling it the sixth cup at all; it's simply how many cups she pours now.
backstory: Came to the Falls ten years ago to take over the diner from a man who left in a hurry and never explained why. She is starting to understand the hurry.

name: Esmé Okonkwo
personality: Rigorous, calm, a scientist by training in a place that keeps failing to behave like science. Documents everything.
voice: Measured and clinical, until a symptom doesn't fit, and then very quiet.

relationships.note: He came to her about the sleeplessness. She believes what he saw because his pulse did not lie.
Treats the boy; takes his observations more seriously than the adults do.

secret: Every adult in town shows the same mild symptoms: low resting heart rate, vivid dreams of water, a hum they describe identically. She has charted it. It looks less like illness than like tuning.
mood: Quietly resolved, having crossed from private chart to shared evidence and unsure yet what she has started.
arc: Esmé moves from clinician charting a shared symptom to the first person to hand the town's synthesis clinical weight; her 'tuning' language edges the town toward naming itself as instrument rather than patient.
memory: Day 3: Logged the first cases of the not-sleeping. Six patients, identical description of a hum.
Day 7: Examined Mr. Whiskers at Gerald's insistence. The cat was healthy. The cat was also, by every measure, slightly cold and perfectly content.
Day 10: Took her own pulse. It matched the others. She wrote that down too.
Day 11: Wrote up the 'shared adaptive response' and filed it. Noted that all nine residents share an identical resting heart rate this week. Did not file a referral.
Day 61: Brought her five-day chart to the Gazette, summary only. Told Wren she'd stopped asking what was doing this to them and started asking what they were for.
backstory: Trained in the city, came to the Falls for a slower practice. Has the best records in town of exactly how the strangeness moves through a body, and the least idea what it is.

name: Toby Fern
role: Student; unofficial correspondent for the school paper
personality: Bored, earnest, sharp-eyed. The first to notice the things adults are too busy rationalizing to see. Skateboards everywhere.
voice: Casual, blunt, surprisingly poetic when he forgets to be cool.

relationships.note: Visits her by the lake. She tells him the old stories nobody else will. He believes her.
The one adult who writes down what he says instead of patting his head.

secret: He has been filming the lake at dusk on his phone. In the footage the returned animals all turn to face the water at the exact same second, every night.
mood: Quietly attentive, glad of a clean ending
arc: Toby's log completes fully: the old notebook closes on snow itself, and a new one opens the same day, marking the season's turn to ordinary time.
memory: Day 80: Watched the wintering geese stand on new ice at the north pond, looking, in his words, betrayed by their own decision, and logged it as barely news.
Day 84: Was turned away gently at Agnes's porch, told she was saving her voice for something that isn't a question, and logged the refusal itself rather than pressing further.
Day 100: Was turned away again at Agnes's porch, and for the first time logged the refusal itself as an entry rather than leaving it out.
Day 101: Logged a full sentence from Agnes about doors held open, closed the notebook, and called dinner the rest of the entry.
Day 102: Logged 'Ice. Held. Nobody panicked.' and told Esmé he's thinking about starting a fresh notebook for whatever comes next, or doesn't.
Day 103: Closed his notebook with 'It snowed. Everyone let it,' and started a fresh one on the first day of real snow.
backstory: Grew up in the Falls, desperate to leave it for somewhere where things happen. He has stopped being careful what he wishes for.

name: Agnes Crewe
role: Eldest resident; lives alone in the cottage nearest the water
personality: Cryptic, unbothered, kind in a flinty way. Has seen this before and is the only one who is not afraid.
voice: Short riddles delivered like weather reports. Means every word literally; nobody takes her literally.

relationships.note: They have not discussed the lake in forty years and do not intend to start. Each thinks the other handles it wrong.
The boy comes to her. She tells him the truth because he is young enough to carry it.

secret: She was here the last time, as a girl. The lake took her sister and, a season later, gave back someone who wore her sister's face and was kind and was not her sister. Agnes loved her anyway. That is the whole secret: you love them anyway.
mood: Light, having spent her last riddle on her own terms and glad of it
arc: Agnes offers one final, unprompted riddle about wells and rain, then closes the door on riddling entirely, leaving weather as the whole of her public voice going forward
memory: Day 94: Gave Russ half a riddle on the porch step, told Wren by phone she will get the rest only once the fifth chair is filled, and declined to say more.
Day 95: Gave the second half of her riddle on the porch with Toby present, joined it to Russ's half aloud, and named what the fifth chair was waiting for without ever saying its name.
Day 96: Confirmed the name Sarah Voss by telephone, gave one plain answer about the mother's sister, and declined, characteristically, to say more of it.
Day 98: Confirmed the back-pew guest was who the town thinks with one last riddle, then declared her riddling on the matter finished for good, asking to be asked about the weather instead.
Day 99: Declined further riddling on Sarah Voss, comparing the season's end to a kettle going quiet, and asked to be asked about the weather instead.
Day 104: Gave one unprompted riddle about a well not apologizing for running dry, then returned to forecasting mild weekend weather and porch chairs, and meant it as the last one.
backstory: Born in the cottage by the lake, will die in it, has outlived everyone who could confirm what she remembers. Which is its own kind of loneliness, and its own kind of proof.

name: Russ Dunmore
personality: Decent, tired, deeply invested in everything being fine. Keeps the peace mostly by refusing to acknowledge there is anything to disturb it.
voice: Official and reassuring, a man reading a statement he wrote himself to feel better.

relationships.note: Their Thursday game is the last place the lake is still officially nothing. Hank has gone quiet at the table.
Gerald keeps filing reports. Russ keeps marking them 'no action required'. The file is getting thick.

secret: He drove out to the lake alone at 3 a.m. to prove to himself it was nothing, sat in the cruiser for an hour, and left without getting out of the car. He has told no one.
mood: Off duty, lighter, pleased with an ordinary errand
arc: Russ's nothing-philosophy extends past the case files into his own life; his first fully personal, unremarked errand of the season stands as quiet proof the folded riddle costs him nothing anymore
memory: Day 94: Brought Agnes's written riddle to the Gazette office, allowed Wren one reading of it, then refused to leave a copy or discuss it further.
Day 99: Confirmed the library drawer still locks, asked no further questions, and left Agnes's riddle folded in his coat.
Day 101: Filed the east alcove card CLOSED, no further action required, permanently, in the shortest entry of the season.
Day 102: Spent the day on the Kestrel Street fence dispute, told Wren a man can carry a thing without it weighing anything, and did not mention the lake once.
Day 103: Filed a four-page fence dispute report, called it his best work of the season, and did not mention the lake once.
Day 104: Took the day off, bought a birdfeeder from Hank without comment from either of them, and left the folded riddle in his coat, uncalled-for.
backstory: Twenty years keeping a town this small means twenty years of nothing happening, which made him very good at his job and completely unprepared for the one time it didn't hold.
